entry.title: Inferring parameters in immune digital twins when the immune system will not sit still

link.title: Inferring parameters in immune digital twins when the immune system will not sit still

entry.content:
Draft notes from my June 2026 talk at Washington State University. Slides here.

The digital twin paradigm rests on three things: a mechanistic software replica of the object, longitudinal data specific to that object, and an inference framework that keeps updating the model as the data arrives. For engineering systems this is hard but tractable. For the immune system it is harder, because the thing you are trying to track is genuinely stochastic — not merely noisily measured.

That distinction matters more than it sounds. If the variability were measurement noise, a well-tuned deterministic estimator would average it away. It is not. The response itself fluctuates, so the parameters you are estimating are moving targets, and an estimator that assumes otherwise will happily converge to a confident wrong answer.

The framework I presented treats the inference step with stochastic adaptive filters instead, so parameter estimates carry uncertainty that reflects the underlying biological variability rather than just the sensor.

To expand: worked example on the HIV model, comparison against batch identification, and what the uncertainty bounds actually mean for a clinician reading them.

entry.title: What set-based analysis tells you about epidemic interventions

link.title: What set-based analysis tells you about epidemic interventions

entry.content:
Draft notes from my October 2024 colloquium at the University of Idaho. Slides here.

Most control formulations of epidemic intervention optimize a single scalar: flatten the peak, or minimize total infections. In practice a public health authority is holding two constraints at once — keep the infected peak prevalence below whatever the hospital system can absorb, and keep the epidemic final size down — while the intervention itself carries a cost that grows the longer it runs.

A set-based dynamic analysis of SIR-type systems makes the trade-off visible rather than implicit. Instead of asking “what is the optimal control signal,” you ask which regions of state space can still reach an acceptable outcome, and what a finite-duration intervention does to that region.

The practical payoff is that finite-time social distancing measures — the only kind anyone actually implements — can be placed rather than merely sized. Timing turns out to matter as much as intensity.

To expand: the invariant set construction, and how this fed into the switched NMPC formulation in the Annual Reviews in Control paper.
